categories.name: Selected exam questions 2018–2019
categories.description: The questions from the selected 2018 and 2019 exams, rewritten as multiple choice. Based on the provided answers.

questions.question: What is the optimization objective of an SVM?
options: Minimize the number of support vectors
Maximize the margin
Maximize the likelihood of the training data
Minimize the squared error

questions.question: What are the support vectors?
options: The weight vector and bias of the hyperplane
The training samples closest to the separating hyperplane
All misclassified samples
The principal components of the data
questions.note: The margin is the distance between the decision boundary and these closest samples.

questions.question: How does changing the width of the margin between classes affect modelling?
options: Large margins tend to give lower generalization error; small margins are more prone to overfitting
Small margins always give the best test accuracy
The margin width has no effect on generalization
Large margins are more prone to overfitting

questions.question: Match each part of the data to its role.

choices.text: Measure performance to tune hyperparameters / choose a model
Measure performance on unseen data (final estimate)

questions.question: You only have a few samples. How should you handle model selection?
options: Use a single small validation set
Use k-fold cross-validation instead of one fixed validation split
Skip validation and only use the test set
Train on the test set too
questions.note: Cross-validation lets every sample be used for both training and validation, which gives a more reliable estimate when data is scarce.

questions.question: What is nested cross-validation used for?
options: Speeding up training
Selecting among different machine learning algorithms with a close to unbiased error estimate
Imputing missing values
Choosing the number of principal components only

questions.question: How is nested cross-validation structured?
options: Outer loop: k-fold CV to tune hyperparameters; inner loop: one test split
Outer loop: k-fold CV splitting into training and test folds; inner loop: k-fold CV on each training fold to select the model
Two independent k-fold CVs whose scores are averaged
One k-fold CV repeated with different random seeds
questions.note: After selecting the model in the inner loop, its performance is evaluated on the outer test fold.

questions.question: We want to know if a regression model (hours spent on assignments → grade) misses something. Which tool helps find un-modelled phenomena?
options: A confusion matrix
A residual plot (residuals versus predicted values)
An ROC curve
A correlation matrix of the features

questions.question: What can a residual plot help detect?
options: Non-linearity that the model does not capture
Outliers
Whether the errors are randomly distributed
The optimal number of trees in a forest

questions.question: Match each regularized regression method to its penalty.

choices.text: L2 penalty: sum of squared weights
L1 penalty: sum of absolute weights

questions.question: Which of Ridge, LASSO and Elastic Net can work as a feature selection technique on its own?
options: Only Ridge
LASSO (and Elastic Net, through its L1 part)
None of them
Only Ridge and Elastic Net
questions.note: The L1 term can set weights exactly to zero, giving sparse models. Ridge only makes weights less extreme.

questions.question:
Two logistic regression models (L1 and L2 regularization) were evaluated over repeated train–test splits, plotted against the inverse regularization parameter C (from $10^{-3}$ to $10^0$):
- L2: training accuracy rises from 0.612 to 0.616; test accuracy peaks around 0.612 for C between $10^{-2.5}$ and $10^{-1.5}$, then drops to 0.611.
- L1: training accuracy rises from 0.606 to 0.616; test accuracy peaks at about 0.6137 for C slightly above $10^{-2}$, then drops to 0.611.
- For C below about $2\cdot 10^{-3}$ both test accuracies fall sharply (to 0.605–0.607).

Which regularization and approximately which C would you choose for future predictions?
options: L2 with C = 1
L1 with C slightly above $10^{-2}$
questions.note: L1 has the best test accuracy there, and the gap to training accuracy is smallest. The differences are small, though; too small C (< $10^{-3}$) clearly hurts.

questions.question:
Two logistic regression models (L1 and L2 regularization) were evaluated over repeated train–test splits, plotted against the inverse regularization parameter C (from $10^{-3}$ to $10^0$):
- L2: training accuracy rises from 0.612 to 0.616; test accuracy peaks around 0.612 for C between $10^{-2.5}$ and $10^{-1.5}$, then drops to 0.611.
- L1: training accuracy rises from 0.606 to 0.616; test accuracy peaks at about 0.6137 for C slightly above $10^{-2}$, then drops to 0.611.
- For C below about $2\cdot 10^{-3}$ both test accuracies fall sharply (to 0.605–0.607).

What happens for large C (close to 1)?
options: Both models underfit
The gap between training and test accuracy grows: the models overfit slightly
Test accuracy is at its maximum
Training accuracy decreases
questions.note: C is the inverse regularization strength, so large C means weak regularization.

questions.question: What are L2 and L1 regularization shrinking, and which can lead to variable selection?
options: L2 shrinks the L2-norm and L1 the L1-norm of the coefficients; L1 can set coefficients to 0 (variable selection)
Both shrink the bias term; L2 does variable selection
L1 shrinks the number of samples; L2 the number of features
Both shrink the learning rate; neither does variable selection

questions.question: How would you explain precision to someone not familiar with machine learning?
options: Of all samples predicted positive, how large a proportion is actually positive
Of all actual positives, how large a proportion was predicted positive
The proportion of all predictions that are correct
How often negatives are predicted negative

questions.question: How would you explain recall to someone not familiar with machine learning?
options: Of all samples predicted positive, how many are actually positive
Of all actual positive samples, how large a proportion was found (predicted positive)
The share of negatives among all samples
The area under the ROC curve

questions.question:
Three one-versus-all confusion matrices (rows = true class, columns = predicted class; first row/column negative, second positive):
Class 1: TN = 21, FP = 4, FN = 2, TP = 13
Class 2: TN = 29, FP = 6, FN = 1, TP = 4
Class 3: TN = 15, FP = 5, FN = 6, TP = 14

Compute the micro-averaged precision and recall (3 decimals).
questions.note: Sum over the matrices first: TP = 13 + 4 + 14 = 31, FP = 4 + 6 + 5 = 15, FN = 2 + 1 + 6 = 9. Precision = 31/46, recall = 31/40.

questions.question:
Three one-versus-all confusion matrices (rows = true class, columns = predicted class; first row/column negative, second positive):
Class 1: TN = 21, FP = 4, FN = 2, TP = 13
Class 2: TN = 29, FP = 6, FN = 1, TP = 4
Class 3: TN = 15, FP = 5, FN = 6, TP = 14

Compute the macro-averaged precision and recall (3 decimals).
questions.note: Compute per class, then average: precision = (13/17 + 4/10 + 14/19)/3, recall = (13/15 + 4/5 + 14/20)/3.

questions.question: What is the difference between micro and macro averaging?
options: Micro sums the matrices first so every sample counts equally; macro averages per-class metrics so every class counts equally (down-weights large classes, suitable for unbalanced data)
Micro is for binary problems only; macro for multiclass
They always give the same result
Macro sums the matrices first; micro averages per class

questions.question:
AdaBoost lines in random order:
A: For j in m boosting rounds
B: Predict class labels $\hat y = \text{predict}(C_j, X)$
C: Set w to uniform weights, $\sum w_i = 1$
D: Compute coefficient $\alpha_j = 0.5\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$
E: Compute the final prediction $\hat y = (\sum_j \alpha_j\,\text{predict}(C_j, X) > 0)$
F: Normalize weights to sum to 1
G: Update weights $w := w\times\exp(-\alpha_j\hat y y)$
H: Train a weighted weak learner $C_j = \text{train}(X, y, w)$
I: Compute weighted error rate $\varepsilon = w\cdot(\hat y \ne y)$

What is the correct order?
options: C, A, H, B, I, D, G, F, E
A, C, H, B, D, I, F, G, E
C, A, B, H, I, D, F, G, E
C, H, A, B, I, G, D, F, E

questions.question: What does a ROC curve show?
options: Precision versus recall
True positive rate versus false positive rate as the decision threshold varies
Training versus test accuracy
Loss versus number of iterations

questions.question: What happens as you trace a ROC curve from the lower left to the upper right?
options: The threshold is lowered: more and more samples are predicted positive, first raising TPR, then also FPR, until everything is predicted positive (TPR = FPR = 1)
The threshold is raised: fewer samples are predicted positive
The number of training samples increases
The model complexity increases
questions.note: In the lower left corner all samples are predicted negative.

questions.question: Which statements about ROC curves are correct?
options: A perfect classifier goes straight up the left side to the top left corner, then along the top
A curve below the diagonal is worse than random guessing
The diagonal corresponds to random guessing
An AUC of 0.97 is worse than random guessing

questions.question: A ROC curve lies only slightly above random guessing. Which technique could leverage such a low-performing model?
options: k-nearest neighbours
Boosting, since this is a weak learner
Removing the regularization
Increasing the test set size

questions.question: Match each function to the classifier it belongs to.
questions.note: Perceptron: 2. Adaline: 1 and 4. Logistic regression: 3 and 5.

questions.question: How does gradient descent search for the minimum of a cost function?
options: It iteratively moves the parameters a step in the opposite direction of the gradient
It moves in the direction of the gradient
It tries all parameter values on a grid
It solves for the point where the cost is zero

questions.question:
Consider this analysis:
Step 3: X = concat(df.iloc[:, 2:10], get_dummies(df['spy_network'], drop_first=True)); y = df.iloc[:, 0]
Step 4: train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.30, stratify=y, random_state=1)

What does get_dummies(df['spy_network'], drop_first=True) do?
options: Standardizes the spy_network column
One-hot encodes spy_network, dropping one category to avoid collinearity
Removes rows with missing spy_network
Label-encodes spy_network as integers

questions.question: How does the perceptron classify a sample?
options: The features are weighted and summed (including a bias), and a threshold decides the class
It finds the nearest training samples
It computes a probability with the sigmoid function
It builds a series of questions

questions.question: How are the perceptron weights updated?
options: After every sample, by the gradient of the squared error
When a sample is misclassified: (true class − predicted class) × input × learning rate is added
Only once, after seeing all samples
By averaging the inputs of each class
questions.note: $\Delta w_j = \eta\,(y^{(i)} - \hat y^{(i)})\,x_j^{(i)}$, which is zero for correctly classified samples.

questions.question: What distinguishes supervised from unsupervised learning?
options: Supervised learning uses labelled data to learn patterns optimal for predicting a response; unsupervised looks for systematic patterns (e.g. maximal variation) in unlabelled data
Supervised learning needs no training data
Unsupervised learning is always more accurate
Supervised learning is only for regression
questions.note: Unsupervised learning is used for compression or exploratory analysis, supervised mostly for prediction.

questions.question: What is the role of PCA in a classification or regression pipeline, and what does its hyperparameter control?
options: It compresses the features into fewer components spanning most of the variation (hopefully removing noise); the hyperparameter is the number of components
It selects samples; the hyperparameter is the test size
It classifies the data; the hyperparameter is C
It imputes missing values; the hyperparameter is the strategy

questions.question: Why would you regularize a model?
options: To reduce overfitting by penalizing large weights, giving more robust, generalizing models
To make training faster
To increase the number of features
To make the training error as small as possible
questions.note: Without regularization, models can produce large, unstable weights that cancel out and fit the training data too closely.

questions.question: What does majority voting mean in classification?
options: The final class is the most common prediction among an ensemble of predictions
The class with the most training samples is always predicted
Each feature votes for a class
The model with the highest accuracy decides alone

questions.question: How is majority voting used in bagging, and why can bagging be more accurate than a single model?
options: Models are trained on different (bootstrap) subsets and the final prediction is a majority vote; this reduces the influence of outliers and the variance
Models are trained sequentially on the errors of the previous ones
One model votes several times on the same sample
The features vote on which model to use

questions.question: How does KNN use majority voting, and why is it resource demanding for very large training sets?
options: The predicted class is the most common among the K neighbours; the whole training set must be stored and searched for every prediction
It votes among K trees; training takes long
It votes among K features; it needs many epochs
It votes among K classifiers; it needs a GPU

questions.question: What is One-vs-Rest (OvR / OvA)?
options: Extending a binary classifier to multiclass by training one classifier per class, with that class as positive and all others as negative
Training one classifier for every pair of classes
Removing all classes but one
Using one feature per class

questions.question: How is a new sample classified with OvR applied to the perceptron?
options: Compute the net input z of every class's classifier and choose the class with the largest z
Choose the first classifier that predicts +1
Average the weights and apply one threshold
Use majority vote over the features

categories.name: Exam-style practice questions
categories.description: New questions in the style of the selected 2018–2019 exams.

questions.question: In a soft-margin SVM, what is the effect of the slack variables?
options: They allow some samples inside the margin or misclassified, controlled by C
They remove the bias term
They make the boundary nonlinear
They set some weights to zero

questions.question: Which statement about the kernel trick is correct?
options: It computes inner products in a high-dimensional feature space without computing the mapping explicitly
It reduces the number of features
It is only used for decision trees
It replaces the hinge loss with log-loss

questions.question: In 5-fold cross-validation, how many times is each sample used for validation?
questions.note: Each fold is the validation fold exactly once; each sample is used for training 4 times.

questions.question: What is leave-one-out cross-validation?
options: k-fold CV with k equal to the number of samples
Removing one feature at a time
A holdout split with one test sample chosen at random
Nested CV with one outer fold

questions.question: A dataset has 400 samples. How many end up in the test set with train_test_split(test_size=0.25)? And with 10-fold CV on the remaining samples, how many are in each validation fold?
A grid search tunes 4 values of C and 3 values of gamma with cv=5. How many models are fitted during the search (excluding the final refit)?
questions.note: $4 \cdot 3 = 12$ combinations, each fitted 5 times.

questions.question: After GridSearchCV has been fitted with the default refit=True, what is best_estimator_?
options: The best parameter combination, refit on the whole training data passed to fit
The model from the best fold only
The test set accuracy
A list of all fitted models

questions.question: A residual plot shows a clear U-shaped (curved) pattern. What does this suggest, and how could you correct it?
options: The relationship is non-linear; add non-linear terms (e.g. polynomial features) or use a non-linear model
The model is perfect
There are too many features; remove some
The test set is too small

questions.question: The spread of the residuals grows with the predicted value (a funnel shape). What is this called?
options: Non-constant error variance (heteroscedasticity)
Multicollinearity
Underfitting
Data leakage

questions.question: In scikit-learn's LogisticRegression, how does the parameter C relate to the regularization strength $\lambda$?
options: C = $1/\lambda$: smaller C means stronger regularization
C = $\lambda$: larger C means stronger regularization
C is the learning rate
C is the number of classes

questions.question: A validation curve shows training accuracy 0.99 and test accuracy 0.75 for a large C, and 0.88 vs 0.86 for a smaller C. Which C would you choose?
options: The large C, because the training accuracy is highest
The smaller C, because it generalizes better (higher test accuracy, smaller gap)
Either, they are equivalent
Neither; increase C further

questions.question: Which method combines L1 and L2 penalties, with a parameter that sets the mix between them?
options: Elastic Net
Ridge
LASSO
PCA

questions.question: A binary classifier gives TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30. Compute the metrics (3 decimals).
questions.note: Precision = 40/50, recall = 40/60, accuracy = 70/100, F1 = 2PR/(P+R) ≈ 0.727.

questions.question: In cancer screening, missing a sick patient is much worse than a false alarm. Which metric is most important?
options: Precision
Recall
Specificity
Accuracy
questions.note: Recall measures how many of the actual positives are found.

questions.question: For a spam filter, putting real emails in the spam folder is much worse than letting some spam through. Which metric matters most (spam = positive)?
options: Recall
Precision
False negative rate
None
questions.note: Precision measures how many emails marked as spam really are spam.

questions.question: A dataset has 950 negatives and 50 positives. A model predicts everything as negative. What is its accuracy, and why is it misleading?
options: 95%, but the recall for the positive class is 0
50%, it is random
5%, it is useless
100%, it never makes mistakes

questions.question: What does an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.5 indicate?
options: A perfect classifier
Performance equal to random guessing
Worse than random guessing
50% precision

questions.question: Which point of the ROC space corresponds to a perfect classifier?
options: (FPR, TPR) = (0, 0)

questions.question: In AdaBoost a weak learner has weighted error rate $\varepsilon = 0.25$. Compute its coefficient $\alpha = 0.5\ln\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$ (3 decimals).
In AdaBoost, what happens to the weights of misclassified samples after a boosting round?
options: They increase, so the next weak learner focuses on them
They decrease
They are set to zero
They stay the same
questions.note: With $w := w\exp(-\alpha\hat y y)$, a misclassified sample has $\hat y y = -1$, so its weight is multiplied by $e^{\alpha} > 1$.

questions.question: Bagging versus boosting.
statements: Bagging trains its models independently (in parallel) on bootstrap samples.
Boosting trains its models sequentially, each focusing on the previous errors.
Boosting can only be used with k-NN.

questions.question: Perceptron update with $\eta = 0.1$: a sample $\mathbf x = (2, -1)$ with true label $y = 1$ is predicted $\hat y = -1$. Compute the weight changes.
questions.note: $\Delta w = \eta(y - \hat y)\mathbf x = 0.1\cdot 2\cdot(2, -1)$, $\Delta b = 0.1\cdot 2 = 0.2$.

questions.question: When is the perceptron guaranteed to converge?
options: Always
When the classes are linearly separable (and the learning rate is small enough)
Only with standardized features
Only for more than two classes

questions.question: How does Adaline's weight update differ from the perceptron's?
options: Adaline uses the continuous linear activation (net input) to compute the error and updates by gradient descent on the squared error; the perceptron uses the thresholded class label
Adaline uses the sigmoid function
Adaline does not use a learning rate
There is no difference

questions.question: OvR perceptron with 4 classes: the net inputs for a new sample are $z_1 = -0.3$, $z_2 = 1.2$, $z_3 = 0.8$, $z_4 = -1.5$. How many classifiers were trained, and which class is predicted?
questions.note: One classifier per class; choose the largest net input.

questions.question: Five classifiers predict the classes A, B, A, C, A for a sample. How many votes does the winning class get? (Answer with the number of votes.)
questions.note: A wins with 3 of 5 votes.

questions.question: Which statements about PCA are correct?
options: It is unsupervised (it does not use the labels)
The principal components are orthogonal and ordered by explained variance
Features should usually be standardized first
It always improves classification accuracy

questions.question: What is the difference between PCA and LDA?
options: PCA finds directions of maximal variance without labels; LDA uses the labels to find directions that separate the classes
LDA is unsupervised; PCA is supervised
They are the same method
PCA is a classifier; LDA is a regression method

questions.question: Which of these is an unsupervised task?
options: Predicting house prices from features
Grouping customers into segments without known labels
Classifying emails as spam
Predicting exam grades from hours studied

questions.question: In a pipeline make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=2), LogisticRegression()), how do you refer to the number of components in a param_grid?
options: 'n_components'
'pca__n_components'
'PCA.n_components'
'pca_n_components'
questions.note: make_pipeline names each step after its lowercase class name.

questions.question: Why should the StandardScaler be inside the pipeline that is passed to GridSearchCV?
options: So it is fit only on the training folds, avoiding information leakage from the validation folds
Because GridSearchCV cannot run without it
It makes the grid search faster
So that the test set is scaled with its own statistics
